objectives:
Comp History

This course introduces freshmen to the basic skills of critical thinking required in the study of English literature, cultural studies, and critical theory. It does so through a dialectic analysis of key concepts in Western thought. We will examine the assumptions and premises or major topics regarding the function of poetry in society, with an emphasis on notions of property, possession, and individualism. We will see that poetry occupies a space of radical resistance to the dominant ideologies of any time period. Students are expected to complete readings at home and to bring questions to class (graded course component). The course also introduces students to the basics of how to occupy a college classroom by challenging the instructor and how to engage in argumentative writing (graded course component).
content: At the heart of this experiment and theory and the history of ideas, we will engage with the seeming “inevitability” of contemporary global capitalism. We will question whether notions of labor, alienation, progress, inequality, freedom, and others are as obvious and necessary as they seem.
grading_policy: Students must attend class having completed the readings. Students must bring questions on card to class each week. This activity and a writing activity every three weeks will amount to 50% of the grade. Another 20％ will be determined through an in-class midterm exam, through which students will be asked to define and identify several key terms discussed in the first half of the course, and to compose a very short essay (500 words). The final 30％ of the class will be determined through a final paper of 4-5 pages (double spaced, 12-point Times New Roman), which students will write by building on one of several provided essay topics or by determining their own topic with the Professor’s assistance.
